clinicalPearls: Thelaziasis is infestation of the eye by Thelazia nematodes, transmitted by fruit-feeding flies that deposit larvae in the conjunctival secretions
Thelazia callipaeda predominates across parts of Asia and Europe, while Thelazia californiensis occurs in North America
Adult worms live in the conjunctival sac, under the eyelids and around the lacrimal apparatus
Symptoms include foreign-body sensation, excessive tearing, conjunctival redness, itching and sometimes visible moving worms
Complications may include keratitis, corneal ulceration and, rarely, more serious ocular damage
Diagnosis is clinical, by directly visualising and removing the slender white worms during slit-lamp or eyelid examination
Treatment is mechanical removal of the worms, with topical measures to relieve irritation and treat any secondary infection
reference.pathophysiology: Thelaziasis results from the deposition of infective Thelazia larvae onto the conjunctiva by drosophilid flies that feed on lacrimal secretions. The larvae mature into adult worms within the conjunctival sac and adnexal structures, where their movement and cuticular surface mechanically irritate the ocular surface. This provokes reflex tearing, conjunctival inflammation and a foreign-body reaction; persistent presence of worms can lead to keratitis and corneal ulceration. Because the parasite remains largely superficial in the eye, disease is usually localised rather than systemic.
additionalDifferentials: Foreign body on the ocular surface
Other ocular parasitoses such as loiasis or ocular larva migrans
Dry eye disease with surface irritation
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of the conjunctival sac and eyelid margins to identify worms
Careful eversion of the eyelids to inspect the fornices
Morphological identification of extracted worms under microscopy
Ocular surface staining to detect corneal involvement
Conjunctival swab if secondary bacterial infection is suspected
Molecular identification of the species where available
redFlags: Corneal ulceration or visual impairment suggesting keratitis
Severe or persistent ocular pain and photophobia
Signs of secondary bacterial infection with purulent discharge
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent once the worms are removed, with rapid symptomatic relief and full recovery unless corneal damage has already occurred.
pitfalls: Treating persistent conjunctivitis as allergic or bacterial without inspecting for worms
Incomplete removal leaving residual worms and continuing symptoms
Overlooking the fornices and lacrimal region where worms hide
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
